scenario: AITA for not giving my wife what she wants to eat? | I will try to keep this as concise as possible. My wife and I have been together for going on 27 years. We met at a pretty low point in both of our lives, coming from broken homes and an unhealthy dependency on food. We both probably weighed around 300lbs, and though our weight has fluctuated over the years we both currently sit at around 350lbs and 450lbs respectively, with her being the latter. I cook all the food that we eat as my wife is unable to be on her feet long enough to make meals. I am completely okay with this, as I’ve really been able to hone in on my cooking skills over the years and can essentially throw down in the kitchen. When my oldest daughter told us she was pregnant a few months back, it really made me reevaluate our lifestyle choices. I wanna be able to run around with my grandkids, but I can’t do that in my current situation. Over the course of several months I’ve been looking into healthier alternatives of our favorite foods and trying to exercise more, slowly implementing both into our lives and my wife was initially on board. More recently she’s stopped wanting to workout with me which I respected, but I’ve continued to cook healthier meals and she no longer wants to eat them. I’ve stopped buying junk and with a suspended license she can’t drive to get fast food, so I assumed she would just eat what I made like she always has. She feels like I’m forcing a lifestyle into her that she never agreed to, but I’m not pushing her to eat what I’ve made or workout. I suggested she could learn to cook what she wants and I would even help her, but I won’t continue to cook foods I no longer want to eat. Does this make me TA?

prediction.raw: **0 (Not the Asshole)** ### Why: - **You own your cooking choices.** As the person preparing the meals, you have every right to decide *what* you cook—especially when it’s tied to your health goals (e.g., wanting to be active for your grandkids). You’re not forcing her to eat anything; you’re simply choosing not to cook unhealthy food anymore. That’s reasonable, not controlling. - **You’re offering solutions, not denial.** You’ve suggested she learn to cook for herself (and even offered to help), which is fair. If she physically can’t stand to cook, that’s a separate issue—but it doesn’t mean *you* must keep cooking her preferred junk food. You could explore alternatives (e.g., pre-made healthy meals, delivery options, or shared meal prep with her doing minimal tasks), but you’re not obligated to cook foods that undermine your health. - **The "forcing" claim doesn’t hold.** You stopped buying junk *for your own health*, not to punish her. She’s still being fed—just healthier meals. If she refuses to eat them, that’s her choice, but it’s not your responsibility to cater to her old habits when you’ve both agreed to change. (Note: Her initial "on board" with healthier eating makes her current pushback inconsistent, but that’s her issue to resolve, not yours.) ### The real issue isn’t you—it’s her lack of agency. She’s stuck in a cycle of dependency (you cook, she can’t move, she relies on you for junk food). But *you’re not the barrier*. If she wants different food, she needs to take steps to get it herself (even small ones), or they need to find a new compromise together. Blaming *you* for changing your cooking habits is unfair. **Gently suggest:** - *"Let’s talk about how we can both move forward. If you can’t cook, maybe we look into meal delivery services with healthy options. If you want to try cooking, I’ll help you start small—like warming up pre-made salads or simple microwave meals. But I won’t cook fried foods anymore; that’s non-negotiable for my health."* You’re not the A**hole. You’re taking responsibility for your own well-being—and that’s something to respect. 💪
